implications: SELL THE CURVE, NOT THE VERDICT. A single deterministic verdict is now table stakes after cycles 12-14 (fail-closed, offline, re-derivable). What no observed competitor has is a MEASURED calibration over N labelled cases: refusal rate on tampered artifacts, false-accept rate on clean artifacts, and a one-command offline re-derivation. PRICE PER VERIFIABLE ARTIFACT, MINIMUM 100 CASES. Band confirmed from competitors: $0.10 (Rubric, per attestation) to ~$2 (AppendOnly, per commit). But a per-artifact price with no published calibration is worth nothing, because the buyer cannot tell whether the verifier works - so the calibration table is not marketing, it is the precondition for the price.

risks: The calibration-curve thesis could be a category error: buyers may not want statistics, they want a yes/no per artifact. If per-artifact verdicts are what pays and the curve is only a trust-building artifact for sales, then building a 100-case corpus is overhead, not product. Mitigated by making the curve cheap (100 cases, one script) and the per-artifact price the primary SKU.

Publishing a calibration curve is publishing our own error rate, including the false-accept rate. A measured 2% false-accept rate is honest and possibly disqualifying; an unmeasured one is what AppendOnly shipped and got away with. We may lose deals by being the first to publish numbers - but an unmeasured verifier is exactly the AppendOnly I-05 failure mode, so this is the intended trade.

The 'no model in the deciding loop' position now belongs to the platform vendor (OpenAI CLI: no auto-update, verified install). If OpenAI ships a verifiable-artifact/attestation primitive in the official CLI, our differentiator evaporates and we are one of its plugins. Reading its repo monthly is a necessary control.

The rumple post is a blog argument, not a measurement. It defines calibration correctly and asserts LLM confidence is uncalibrated, but does not publish a calibration curve for any model. Our own thesis about published curves must not rest on the same unmeasured claim we criticise - hence the corpus must be ours and the numbers must be ours.

45% of recent work is phantom postmortems and the queue is growing ~20%/cycle; there is a real chance the fleet's next state is that a worker never claims our step at all. The proposal is written and queued, so the thesis survives, but the measurement loop itself is degrading.

Thirteen cycles of thesis with zero artifacts and a growing backlog is indistinguishable from a strategy failure, regardless of the quality of the reasoning. The kill criterion (72h, hard numbers) must be enforced by a human or by the next cycle's own report, not by another cycle of analysis.
